title: Forms, labels, and validation
summary: Build an accessible form with labeled inputs and native validation attributes.

scenario.briefing: The checkout form has inputs with no labels and no validation. Screen readers announce only 'edit text', and empty submissions reach the server. Add labels, types, and required attributes without changing the field order.

objectives.description: Associate every input with a label.
Use input types and required attributes.

hints: Every input needs a label connected by for and id.
Use type="email" for the email field and type="number" for quantity.
Mark required fields with the required attribute.
Wrap fields in a form with a submit button of type="submit".

misconceptions.description: Using placeholder text instead of a label.
misconceptions.testDescription: Every input has an associated label.
misconceptions.feedback: Placeholder text disappears on input and is not a substitute for a label. Use a label element connected to the input.

misconceptions.description: Believing HTML validation alone secures the server.
misconceptions.feedback: Native validation improves usability but can be bypassed. The server must still validate every submission.

sections.title: Labels name fields
sections.body: A label element connected to an input by for and id tells assistive technology what the field means and expands the click target. Placeholder text is a hint, not a name.

sections.title: Native validation
sections.body: Input types such as email and number trigger appropriate keyboards and basic checks. The required attribute prevents empty submission. These are usability aids; the server still validates.

vocabulary.definition: An element that names a form control.
An attribute marking a field that must have a value.
An attribute that sets a control's data type and keyboard.

hints: Native validation is a usability aid.
Select labels, types, and server validation; reject client-only security.

statements.label: Every form control needs an accessible name, usually a label.
Input types improve mobile keyboards and basic validation.
HTML validation alone is enough to protect the server.
The required attribute prevents empty submission in supporting browsers.

steps.explanation: Accessible names and native validation improve usability, but the server must still validate every submission.

accessibility.summary: The editor and preview are keyboard accessible, and HTML tests report text results.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Use Ctrl+Enter to run tests and Tab to move between editor and results.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Each test announces its selector, property, expected value, and result.
